analysis:
The only change in ProviderLoop.swift is the head-side insertion at lines 484-497. It adds stored-state declarations to the ProviderLoop actor for an add-on hold feature: AddonHoldBook, addonHoldTask, addonHoldGeneration, addonHoldMonitorTask, addonIPCServer, addonHoldPaths, test-seam overrides (addonHoldPathsOverride, addonPeerAuthenticatorOverride, addonHoldNowMs, addonHoldDrainTimeout), and a reference to ProviderLoop.addonHoldDrainTimeoutDefault. These are inert declarations. They carry no logic, no I/O and no authorization behavior, so nothing in this file regresses a threat-model control.

The patch hints at new attack surface in other files that this batch does not include: a local IPC socket (AddonIPCServer) with a peer authenticator, a lease monitor, and a drain-and-unload driver. These live in ProviderLoop+AddonHold and related files. The next review pass should examine:
- Peer authentication on the local socket. This is a TB-003 local-process boundary. Check whether the socket path and permissions are owner-only, and that the default authenticator is not weakened by the test override, which must be absent from production paths.
- Whether add-on holds can induce model unload or admission closure, creating local denial of service against availability. This relates to T-010 and T-029 and to the serving drain logic in `servingDrain`.
- Whether hold bookkeeping interacts safely with update, lifecycle, shutdown and reconnect state. These are the existing fields `isShuttingDown`, `updatePhase` and `lifecycleStatus`.
- Whether any add-on path can read prompt plaintext (A-001) or key material (A-003).

I cannot conclude anything about those behaviors from this diff alone. The base_text for lines 484-497 is unchanged apart from the insertion, and the surrounding code is unaffected. Because the new attack surface sits in unsupplied files, I am flagging it for deeper review rather than reporting a finding.
